passage: I'm Rajni. For two years I told myself I'd start running. I bought shoes, downloaded a plan, and stopped after three days, every time. Last spring my friend Noor asked what usually happened right before I skipped. I thought about it. I'd wake up, check my phone, and forty minutes later I was still in bed scrolling. So I changed small things. The phone went to charge in the kitchen. My running clothes went on the chair by the bed. After each run I let myself have the good coffee, not the instant stuff. It sounds almost silly. But I've run three mornings a week for five months now. The scrolling habit still pulls at me some nights. I just don't give it my mornings anymore.

qa.q: Where did Rajni move the phone to charge?
qa.a: The phone went to charge in the kitchen.

qa.q: How might Rajni have felt on realising what happened before each skipped run?
qa.a: Rajni was probably surprised and a little frustrated to see that forty minutes of scrolling in bed kept eating up the mornings.

qa.q: Why did Rajni's small changes work better than the earlier plans?
qa.a: Rajni removed the cue for scrolling, made running clothes the first thing in sight, and added a reward after each run.

qa.q: How might Noor feel seeing Rajni's progress?
qa.a: Noor might feel pleased that one simple question helped a friend finally change. 😊

grounding: Shows a young adult changing cues, routines and rewards to build a running habit and weaken a scrolling habit.

passage:
Hostel mentor's note, Irawati, second week of term.

Gurpreet came to me asking for help with sleep. He's been staying up past three most nights gaming, then missing morning labs. He was frustrated with himself: 'I start at eleven saying one match.' We talked about what sets off the late nights. He noticed that his roommate starts playing at eleven too, and the sound pulls him in. He decided to go to the reading room from ten, leave his laptop in the cupboard, and play only on weekends with his friends. He asked me to check in with him on Mondays. First week he slipped twice. I told him that was normal and not a reason to quit. This Monday he said he'd made four labs out of five.

qa.q: How many labs did Gurpreet make this week?
qa.a: He made four labs out of five.

qa.q: What was Gurpreet feeling when he said 'I start at eleven saying one match'?
qa.a: He felt frustrated and disappointed in himself for losing control of his nights.

qa.q: How did Irawati support Gurpreet's habit change?
qa.a: Irawati helped him find his trigger, let him choose his own plan and treated slips as normal rather than failures.

qa.q: How might Gurpreet's roommate be part of the change?
qa.a: His roommate's gaming is part of what pulls Gurpreet in, so moving away from the sound makes it easier for him to stick to his plan.

grounding: Shows an adult mentor helping a student spot a cue, change his routine and use a check-in to break a harmful habit.

passage:
Sunday night

Day 21 of no sugary tea at the office. Wasim bet me I wouldn't last a week. 😅

The trick wasn't willpower. I figured out I always went for tea at 4 because I was bored and tired after lunch meetings. So now at 4 I walk around the building once and fill my water bottle. Stupid but it works. I also stopped keeping biscuits in my drawer. If they're not there, I don't eat them.

Two slip days. Both after bad calls. I noticed that. Stress is a cue too.

Maybe next I'll try the same trick for reading before bed. Put the book on my pillow so I have to move it.

Wasim owes me samosas.
— Hemant

qa.q: What does Hemant do at 4 o'clock now?
qa.a: Hemant walks around the building once and fills a water bottle.

qa.q: What did Hemant realise when thinking about the two slip days?
qa.a: Both came after bad calls, which showed Hemant that stress was also a trigger.

qa.q: Why does removing the biscuits from Hemant's drawer help?
qa.a: Without the easy cue in sight, Hemant doesn't have to fight the urge as often.

qa.q: How might Wasim feel about losing the bet?
qa.a: Wasim might grumble about the samosas but also be impressed, since Wasim didn't expect Hemant to last a week.

grounding: Shows a young worker spotting the cues behind a habit and swapping routines to break it.

passage: Between customers at her family's kirana shop in Hajipur, Kalyani used to pick up her phone and lose half an hour to videos. The bank exam was four months away, and her books stayed in a bag under the counter. Her friend Ritu, who had cleared a clerk exam last year, visited one evening and looked around. 'Your phone is on the counter and your book is hidden. Swap them.' So Kalyani kept one thin revision booklet open beside the till, and the phone went into the drawer behind the rice sacks. Her rule: one page per gap between customers. After each chapter she let herself have a cup of the lemon tea she loved from the stall opposite. In the first week she kept reaching for the drawer out of habit. By the third week her hand went to the booklet instead, almost without thinking.

qa.q: Where did Kalyani put her phone?
qa.a: In the drawer behind the rice sacks.

qa.q: How did Kalyani feel when she kept reaching for the drawer in the first week?
qa.a: She was probably frustrated with herself, because the old phone habit pulled at her even though she had chosen the booklet.

qa.q: How did Ritu's suggestion use cues?
qa.a: Making the good habit visible and the bad one hidden changed what Kalyani reached for, while lemon tea after each chapter gave her a reward.

qa.q: How might Ritu feel seeing Kalyani's progress?
qa.a: Pleased that her simple tip helped, and perhaps reminded of her own exam preparation.

grounding: Shows a young woman in a small town redesigning cues and rewards to replace a phone habit with study.

passage: Kaito wanted two things in his second year at university in Sendai: to run in the mornings and to stop the late-night snacking that came with his games. His roommate Yosef, an exchange student from Haifa who studied psychology, drew three boxes on a napkin: cue, routine, reward. "What starts the snacking?" Kaito thought. "The loading screen. I grab chips while it loads." "So move the chips. What starts the running?" "Nothing. I just hope." They set it up that night. Chips on the top shelf in a closed box; a jug of barley tea by the console instead. Running shoes on top of his phone by the door, so he had to touch them to leave. And a reward: a warm melon bun from the bakery at the end of the route, only on running days. The first week was clumsy. By the fourth, his feet found the shoes before his brain was awake.

qa.q: Where did they put the running shoes?
qa.a: On top of his phone by the door.

qa.q: What might Kaito have felt when admitting that nothing started the running, he just hoped?
qa.a: Kaito probably felt a bit sheepish, realising he had been relying on hope and willpower alone.

qa.q: How did they use cue, routine and reward to change both habits?
qa.a: They removed the snacking cue by hiding the chips and adding barley tea, created a running cue with shoes on the phone, and rewarded runs with a melon bun.

qa.q: How might Yosef see Kaito's progress by week four?
qa.a: Yosef would probably feel pleased that the napkin plan worked, seeing the running habit happen almost automatically.

grounding: A student in Japan designs cues, routines and rewards with his roommate to build running and cut late-night snacking.

passage: At the nursing hostel beside the district hospital, Reena's alarm rang at 5:15 for the 7 a.m. shift, and she hit snooze five times, every day. By the time she reached the ward she was rushed and snappish. Sister Kalyani, who ran the ward, noticed and asked on a quiet night shift, "What happens between the alarm and your feet on the floor?" "I reach for the phone to switch it off. Then I start scrolling." "Then the phone is the problem, not you." Reena put an old wind-up alarm clock from her mother across the room and left the phone charging in the common room. She laid her uniform on the chair by the clock, so switching it off meant standing next to her clothes. Her reward was the first cup of mess tea, drunk slowly on the steps before the ward. It took two weeks. Then one morning she realised she hadn't touched snooze at all.

qa.q: How many times did Reena hit snooze every day?
qa.a: Five times.

qa.q: What was Reena feeling when she reached the ward after snoozing?
qa.a: Reena felt rushed and irritable, arriving snappish.

qa.q: How did Reena redesign the morning habit?
qa.a: She moved the alarm across the room, kept the phone out, set her uniform beside it as a cue, and rewarded herself with slow tea on the steps.

qa.q: How might Sister Kalyani see the change?
qa.a: Sister Kalyani would likely feel pleased that one question helped Reena find a fix, and enjoy a calmer trainee on the ward.

grounding: In a nursing hostel, a trainee redesigns her morning cue and reward to break a snooze-and-scroll habit.

passage:
Dear Uma,
You asked how I stopped smoking, since you've started at college and want to stop before it sticks. I'll tell you what worked, not what I'm proud of.
I never decided to smoke; it attached itself to things. Chai at the tapri after class: cigarette. Exam stress: cigarette. So I didn't fight the craving head-on. I changed the cues. I took a different road home that skipped the tapri. I carried saunf and a rubber band to snap when the urge came. I told my friends I'd quit so they stopped offering.
I also saw the college doctor, who talked me through options and checked in every month. That helped more than I expected.
I slipped twice. Both times I started again the next morning instead of giving up. My reward was a jar for the money I'd have spent, for a trip to Hampi. I went in March.
Call me when it's hard.
Pranav Bhaiya

qa.q: Where did Pranav use to smoke after class?
qa.a: At the tapri, with chai.

qa.q: What does Pranav's line about not being proud suggest about his feelings?
qa.a: Pranav feels a little ashamed of having smoked, and wants to be honest rather than boastful.

qa.q: Which of Pranav's changes worked on the cues rather than the craving?
qa.a: Taking a different road that skipped the tapri, and telling friends so they stopped offering, removed the triggers.

qa.q: How might Uma feel reading the letter?
qa.a: Uma would likely feel supported and less alone, seeing a practical plan and an open invitation to call when it's hard.

grounding: A young man writes to a younger student about breaking a smoking habit by changing cues, getting support and using rewards.

passage:
Okay, Disha, you asked how the running happened. So, I'm Wasim, and a year ago I was the person who bought running shoes and used them as a doorstop.

What changed wasn't willpower. I made it stupidly easy. I slept in my running T-shirt. The shoes stayed right beside the bed, laces already loose. The rule was only "put them on and step outside". If I came back after two minutes, that still counted.

And then the reward. There's a tea stall at the end of our lane. I only let myself have the cutting chai there after a run. Sounds silly, but by week three my feet were walking there before my brain woke up.

The harder part was killing the midnight scrolling. I moved my charger to the kitchen. First week, I kept getting up to check the phone and feeling like an idiot. By the second month I was asleep by eleven, and honestly, that did more for the running than anything else.

qa.q: Where did Wasim keep the running shoes?
qa.a: The shoes stayed right beside the bed, laces already loose.

qa.q: What did Wasim feel during the first week of charging the phone in the kitchen?
qa.a: Wasim felt restless and a bit foolish, getting up to check the phone and "feeling like an idiot".

qa.q: What could a friend who wants a new habit borrow from Wasim?
qa.a: Make the first step tiny, put the cue where you cannot miss it, attach a small reward, and move the trigger for a bad habit out of reach.

qa.q: How might Disha, the podcast host, react to hearing that sleeping in a running T-shirt helped?
qa.a: Disha might be amused at first, then see that the plan works because it removes excuses rather than depending on willpower.

grounding: A young adult explains building running and sleep habits by designing cues, tiny routines and rewards, and moving the phone charger to break late-night scrolling.

passage:
My sister Ritu used to drink three energy drinks a day in her first year of engineering. I share the flat with her, so I know the fridge.

In June, something changed. She stuck a paper chart on the fridge door with dates on it. Every day without a can got a green tick. She started keeping a steel bottle of lemon water where the cans had been, on the top shelf, right at eye level. The first week she was snappy in the afternoons and slept at odd hours. I asked if she was okay, and she said, "Headache. It passes." I couldn't tell if she was annoyed at me or at herself.

Then I noticed she'd set a phone alarm for 4 p.m., the time she used to buy a can, and she'd go for a walk to the park instead. By August the chart had a long green line. She hasn't said anything big about it. I'm Chaitanya, and I just stopped buying cans for the fridge too.

qa.q: What did Ritu keep on the top shelf where the cans used to be?
qa.a: She kept a steel bottle of lemon water on the top shelf, at eye level.

qa.q: What might Ritu have been feeling during the first week without cans?
qa.a: Ritu was probably irritable and uncomfortable from the headaches, and maybe annoyed with herself, though Chaitanya could not be sure which.

qa.q: How could Chaitanya keep supporting Ritu's new habit?
qa.a: He can keep the fridge free of cans, notice her green ticks without making a fuss, and perhaps join her 4 p.m. walks.

qa.q: How does watching Ritu affect Chaitanya?
qa.a: Chaitanya is quietly impressed and supportive, and he changes his own habit by no longer buying cans for the fridge.

grounding: A brother observes his sister replacing an energy-drink habit with a new cue, routine and visible reward over a summer.

passage:
Week 1, Tuesday. Kavitha comes home from college at six, lies on the sofa "for five minutes", and scrolls until ten. The revision notes stay in her bag. Abhinav, her study partner, texts: "Did you do the micro chapter?" She doesn't reply.

Week 3, Friday. She has tried something new. Every evening she makes her tea, and the moment the cup is ready she carries it to the desk and opens her notebook, just for one page. The bag now hangs on the chair, not by the door. Some days one page becomes six. Abhinav tests her on the phone for ten minutes after, and she marks each evening with a star on the calendar.

Week 7, Monday. The calendar is full of stars with a few gaps. Kavitha misses two days during a cousin's wedding and panics. Then she opens the notebook with her tea on Wednesday as usual. "Two gaps is not a broken chain," she tells Abhinav. "It's just a gap." ☕

qa.q: What does Kavitha do the moment her tea is ready?
qa.a: She carries it to the desk and opens her notebook, just for one page.

qa.q: How did Kavitha feel when she missed two days during the wedding?
qa.a: She panicked at first, afraid she had ruined the habit, and then felt calmer and more confident when she restarted as usual.

qa.q: What could Kavitha do if the habit slips again?
qa.a: She can go straight back to the tea-and-one-page routine the next day and ask Abhinav to keep testing her, instead of waiting for a fresh start.

qa.q: How is the change felt by Abhinav between week 1 and week 7?
qa.a: In week 1 he is ignored, but by week 7 he is a regular part of her routine, so he feels more useful and less frustrated as a study partner.

grounding: Over seven weeks a student builds an evening revision habit by linking it to tea, starting small and marking progress, and recovers after missed days.

passage:
Ganga, you're asking how I quit smoking when I was your age? It wasn't willpower. It was a trick.
I started at nineteen, in my first job in Kolkata. Every tea break, the whole team went downstairs and smoked. The tea, the stairs, the friends, and the cigarette: all one thing.
I tried to quit four times by just refusing. Failed every time, because at tea break my feet walked me downstairs.
Then a doctor at a free clinic said, "Change the routine, not just the cigarette." So I kept the tea break, but I went up to the roof instead, with a cup of tea and a roasted chana packet. After a month, the craving at tea time faded. I marked each clean day on a calendar and bought myself a book at the end of every month.
Three years clean, then forever. That's your Tanvir Chacha's secret: same cue, new routine.

qa.q: Where did Tanvir go at tea break instead?
qa.a: Up to the roof, with a cup of tea and a roasted chana packet.

qa.q: How did young Tanvir feel after failing to quit four times?
qa.a: Young Tanvir felt frustrated and discouraged, because his feet kept taking him downstairs at tea break.

qa.q: What was the turning point in the story, and why did it work?
qa.a: Following the clinic doctor's advice to change the routine but keep the tea break, because the cue stayed and a new habit replaced the old one.

qa.q: How might the team downstairs have felt when Tanvir stopped joining them?
qa.a: The team may have missed Tanvir or teased Tanvir at first, but likely accepted it over time.

grounding: Illustrates an elder recounting how Tanvir broke a smoking habit by keeping the cue and changing the routine and reward.

passage:
Nilesh wanted to study for the banking exam every morning before his warehouse shift. The problem: he shared one room in Nashik with his sister Deepika and their mother, and Deepika worked late at a call centre, sleeping till nine.
For two weeks he failed. He'd wake at six, see Deepika asleep, feel guilty about switching on the light, and go back to bed.
Then he redesigned it. He moved his books to the building's stairwell landing the night before, so they were waiting there. He set his alarm to vibrate under his pillow. He'd do one practice set on the landing, then reward himself with tea from the stall downstairs, which opened at 6:30.
The first morning was cold and dark. The second, easier. By the third week, his feet went to the stairwell before his brain woke up. Deepika only noticed because the tea stall man started asking for him.

qa.q: Where did Nilesh move his books the night before?
qa.a: To the building's stairwell landing.

qa.q: How did Nilesh feel when he saw Deepika asleep at six?
qa.a: Nilesh felt guilty about switching on the light, so he went back to bed.

qa.q: Which parts of Nilesh's redesign made the habit stick?
qa.a: Books placed ready as a cue, a silent alarm, one set as the routine and tea as the reward, all fitted around the shared room.

qa.q: How might Deepika feel when she learns about Nilesh's mornings?
qa.a: Deepika would probably feel touched that he worked around her sleep, and proud of his effort.

grounding: Shows a young adult designing cue, routine and reward to build a study habit despite a crowded home.

passage:
Rashmi and her flatmate Elizabeth, both new to Mumbai, had developed the same habit: coming home from work, falling onto the sofa, opening their phones, and ordering fried food. By ten they'd feel sluggish and annoyed with themselves.
"We need to break this," Elizabeth said one Sunday.
They looked at what happened. The cue was walking in the door, tired. The routine was sofa, phone, order. The reward was relief.
So they changed the path. They kept a gym bag by the door, and on three evenings they went straight to the building's gym for twenty minutes before sitting down. They stocked the kitchen with quick things: eggs, bread, dal they'd cooked on Sunday. The reward became a proper chat on the balcony with chai.
Some evenings they failed. But after a month, walking in the door made Rashmi think "gym bag" before "sofa".

qa.q: What did they keep by the door?
qa.a: A gym bag.

qa.q: How did Rashmi and Elizabeth feel by ten on the old evenings?
qa.a: They felt sluggish and annoyed with themselves.

qa.q: How did they use cue, routine and reward to change the habit?
qa.a: They kept the cue of walking in tired, swapped the routine for a short gym session and simple food, and replaced the reward with chai and a balcony chat.

qa.q: What would change if only one of them had tried to break the habit?
qa.a: It might have been harder, because the other's ordering and sofa routine would keep pulling them back.

grounding: Illustrates two young adults redesigning cues, routines and rewards to replace a harmful evening habit.

passage:
"You're doing it again," Keerthana said from the doorway.
Uma looked up from her phone, bed unmade, 9:40 a.m. "Doing what?"
"Waking up and scrolling for an hour. You said you wanted to run."
"I do want to. I just... the phone's right there."
"So move it. Charge it in the kitchen. Put your shoes where the phone was."
"That's so simple it's insulting."
"Try it for a week. And pick a reward. What do you like?"
Uma thought. "The good filter coffee from downstairs."
"Coffee only on run days, then."
On day four, Uma knocked on Keerthana's door, red-faced and grinning. "I ran. Sort of. I walked half."
"Still counts."
"And the weird thing? I reached for my phone this morning and grabbed my shoes instead." She held up two cups. "Coffee?"
"Only because you ran."

qa.q: Where did Keerthana suggest Uma charge the phone?
qa.a: In the kitchen.

qa.q: How did Uma feel on day four, and how can you tell?
qa.a: She felt proud and happy, red-faced and grinning even though she walked half of the run.

qa.q: Which parts of Keerthana's plan helped build the new habit?
qa.a: Changing the cue by moving the phone and putting the shoes in its place, and tying a reward, the coffee, to run days only.

qa.q: What might it be like for Keerthana to see the plan work?
qa.a: Keerthana probably feels pleased and amused, happy to share the coffee as a reward for Uma's effort 😊

grounding: Shows a young adult redesigning a cue and a reward to replace a scrolling habit with running.
